A1.justification: Both PDFs describe REPPO with the same authors, core algorithm, and continuous-control benchmarks. All pages, including appendices, equations, tables, and rendered figures, support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original toy optimization experiments, DMC and ManiSkill evaluations, component ablations, and memory and training-stability analyses.

after.justification: v3 reports original continuous-control evaluations, additional gradient-estimator comparisons, and new Atari-10 results for discrete REPPO.

M1.justification: Appendix B introduces D-REPPO, computing finite-action expectations for policy value, entropy, and KL terms instead of differentiating through sampled continuous actions. This substantially extends the procedure to discrete policies. Continuous REPPO retains its principal components; its now-preferred clipped objective was already an optional variant in v1.

E1.justification: v3 adds actual evaluation on ten Atari games with discrete actions, substantially extending coverage beyond continuous locomotion and manipulation. The original 23 DMC tasks, eight ManiSkill tasks, and toy experiment remain. Diffusion policies are discussed but not evaluated.

E2.justification: v3 Figure 4 adds evaluated RPO and DPO comparators, while Appendix B introduces a reported PQN comparison. PPO and FastTD3 reference rows disappear from the component-ablation comparison, although both remain elsewhere. Despite mentioning PPO in the Atari prose, the corresponding Figure 8 and Table 1 report only REPPO and PQN.

E3.justification: v3 introduces gradient-estimator controls and an Atari protocol with human-normalized scores, curves through 200M timesteps, and lambda 0.65 instead of the continuous default 0.95. Table 2 changes the stated critic lower bound from max r/(1-gamma) to min r/(1-gamma), without establishing rerunning. A ManiSkill budget change remains unresolved because Figure 4 labels PPO as 200M while its caption states 100M.

E4.justification: New Section 4.1 compares pathwise REPPO with score-based variants using either learned Q values or PPO-style GAE, directly investigating whether benefits arise from value learning or gradient estimation. The original HL-Gauss, normalization, auxiliary-loss, KL, and buffer-size analyses are retained in Appendix D; their relocation is not an additional experiment.

E5.justification: The reported seed counts increase from 10 to 20 for REPPO and from four to 20 for PPO, substantially increasing stated replication of the central comparisons. FastTD3 remains at five seeds, and the existing 95% bootstrapped confidence-interval practice is retained.

E6.justification: v3 adds estimator-ablation, RPO/DPO, and Atari results. Atari Table 1 reports human-normalized means of 2.98 for REPPO and 3.35 for PQN, with IQM 1.64 for both. Existing benchmark and component-ablation curves also change. The joint objective is now reported slightly worse than clipping, whereas v1 reported no measurable difference. These are revised findings, not established same-setting performance gains across versions.

T1.justification: v3 adds finite-action objective formulas in Equations 18–20 and revises existing mathematical expressions: the TD-lambda normalization changes, and the KL-multiplier update replaces v1's duplicated entropy residual with a KL residual. These are limited algebraic extensions and corrections, without new theorems or proofs. The HL-Gauss equations are relocated from Appendix A to Section 3.3.

C1.justification: The central claims about on-policy value learning, joint entropy/KL tuning, stability, and efficiency remain. The introduction removes the continuous-action qualification from its first contribution and tempers its comparison with tuned baselines from superiority to competitiveness. The conclusion retains essentially the same principal contributions.

C2.justification: Section 4.1 newly distinguishes benefits of learned Q values from pathwise estimation, discusses applicability to non-reparameterizable policies, and attributes difficulties with GAE-based tuning to variance. Appendix B adds qualified explanations involving exploration and Atari return variance. v3 also acknowledges undiscounted empirical state occupancy and expands the framework-specific limitations of wall-clock comparisons.

D1.justification: Most architecture, optimizer, normalization, and code-access information is retained. v3 corrects the documented critic lower-bound rule, supplies the Atari lambda exception, and expands the JAX/PyTorch runtime discussion with sampling and CPU-related details. Atari-specific architecture and preprocessing information remain sparse.

R1.justification: v3 substantively expands positioning around joint entropy/KL optimization, projection-based trust regions, and differentiable trust-region layers, including Akrour et al. and Otto et al. It adds relationships to discrete SAC and diffusion policies and changes PQN unification from future work to an evaluated extension. The retained reliable-success metric also receives new attribution to Chan et al.

P1.justification: v3 extensively rewrites and condenses the introduction, background, and method exposition. It reorganizes the algorithm around value learning, policy learning, and architectures, places estimator comparisons first in the evaluation, moves HL-Gauss mathematics into the main text, and regroups implementation details and existing analyses within the appendices.

P2.justification: v3 adds an estimator schematic, a gradient-comparison figure, and Atari plots and a results table. The component ablation is split into separate batch-size panels and relocated. The selected-task main-text grid disappears while full per-task appendix plots remain. Existing figures receive substantial rearrangement, legend changes, and revised axes, including 50M rather than 200M timestep ranges in the continuous-control appendix plots.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the central empirical argument: Section 4.1 separates value-learning and estimator effects that v1's comparisons between complete algorithms could not isolate. Increased reported replication and additional baselines further improve confidence in that argument, while Atari results test a meaningful extension. Reproducibility remains imperfect: Algorithm 1 differs from the preferred clipped objective, the discrete entropy sign conflicts with the continuous loss, and ManiSkill horizon labels disagree. These issues limit the gains but do not outweigh the substantially stronger evidence for the main contribution.
